title: Volume

findings.finding: Compare two prisms to explain why an end profile does not determine prism depth.
findings.breakdown: The task extends the existing construction question by asking students to explain which views depend on the distance between the ends.
findings.checked: The worked examples teach front, back, side and top views, including reversal of an asymmetric end profile. For two right prisms with the same end profile and orientation but different positive depths, corresponding front and back views remain unchanged; side and top views change in their depth dimension. No additional mathematical method is needed.
findings.assumptions: Both prisms retain the same orientation, with their end faces at the front and back. Compare corresponding views at the same scale.

repair.proposal: After Question 3, offer this optional extension: Use the end face in Question 3(d). Sketch two right prisms with this same end face and orientation but different distances between their front and back faces. Which corresponding front, back, side and top views stay the same, and which change? Explain why the end face alone cannot determine that distance. Expected answer: the front views match, and the back views match. The side and top views change in the depth direction. The end profile fixes the shape and size of the ends but does not specify their separation.

findings.doneWhen: Students construct two different depths while preserving the end profile and explain correctly which corresponding views remain unchanged.

findings.finding: Connect a triangular prism's side view with its different internal sections.
findings.breakdown: The task asks students to explain why a projected view does not determine every cross-section.
findings.checked: p3 supplies the rectangular side view. p10 explicitly demonstrates rectangular longitudinal sections and triangular sections parallel to the ends. Both proposed section shapes are correct for non-degenerate cuts through the right triangular prism.
findings.assumptions: Cuts pass through the interior; a longitudinal cutting plane is parallel to a rectangular side face.

repair.proposal: After p12-q2, offer: “Return to the triangular prism in p3-example-perspective. Its side view is a rectangle. Must every cross-section also be a rectangle? Give two different section shapes and describe the cutting planes.” Expected answer: No. A cut parallel to a triangular end gives a congruent triangle; an interior longitudinal cut parallel to a rectangular side gives a rectangle. A view projects the solid, whereas a cross-section shows the region exposed by a cut.

findings.doneWhen: The optional task connects views and sections using only the geometry already demonstrated.

findings.finding: Hold the container's base fixed while varying water volume to expose the relationship between volume and depth.
findings.breakdown: The existing p40-q18 parts change container shape and base area; the proposed run isolates volume while keeping base area constant.
findings.checked: p19 teaches rectangular-prism volume, p33 teaches litre-to-cubic-centimetre conversion, and p40-q18 already requires finding water depth. The fixed base area is 200 cm², giving depths 5, 10, 15 and 20 cm, all below the 30 cm container height. The follow-up gives 3000 ÷ 400 = 7.5 cm.
findings.assumptions: Containers have vertical sides and horizontal bases; dimensions describe their interiors.

repair.proposal: After p40-q18 and before p40-q19, insert: A rectangular container has an internal horizontal base 20 cm by 10 cm and height 30 cm. Before calculating, predict how the depths compare when it contains (a) 1 L, (b) 2 L, (c) 3 L and (d) 4 L. Calculate each depth and explain the pattern. Expected depths: 5 cm, 10 cm, 15 cm and 20 cm. With base area fixed, depth is proportional to volume. Follow with: A different rectangular container has an internal horizontal base 25 cm by 16 cm and height 15 cm. It contains 3 L. Find the water depth. Expected answer: 7.5 cm.

findings.doneWhen: The run includes prediction, explanation and the unpatterned follow-up, with only water volume changing within the run.

findings.finding: Explain when horizontal surface area multiplied by a fall in water level gives the lost volume.
findings.breakdown: The task generalises the 75 cm fall and identifies the point at which the shallow end becomes dry.
findings.checked: p40-q20 models a trapezoidal-prism pool with a straight sloping floor. For 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 m, the removed water occupies a rectangular layer across the full 50 m by 25 m footprint. For x = 1.2 m, part of that proposed layer lies below the shallow floor, so 50 × 25 × x overcounts. Explaining this needs only the taught prism geometry and volume formula.
findings.assumptions: The pool starts full, has vertical walls and a straight floor sloping from 1 m to 2 m depth, as in p40-q20's intended model.

repair.proposal: After p40-q20-c, offer: The pool starts full. Its water level falls by x metres. For which values of x can the lost volume be calculated as 50 × 25 × x cubic metres? Explain why this calculation fails for a fall of 1.2 m. Expected answer: 0 ≤ x ≤ 1. Up to a 1 m fall, the removed layer extends across the whole horizontal footprint. Beyond 1 m, the shallow end is dry, and part of the proposed rectangular layer lies below the pool floor.

findings.doneWhen: The optional task gives the interval including its endpoints and explains the failure beyond 1 m without requiring a new calculation method.

findings.finding: All introductory end views appear symmetric, so copying the front view unchanged produces the correct back view without exposing the required left-right reversal. Independent practice then requires that distinction for asymmetric ends.
findings.breakdown: A student using the plausible rule 'the back view is an unchanged copy of the front' would retain the right triangle's vertical leg, the L shape's tall leg or the pentagon's cut-off corner on the wrong side. The first independent question already requires this unmodelled distinction.
findings.checked: Checked all supplied teaching, which is complete. The worked triangle, guided rectangle and guided house profile do not visibly distinguish copying from horizontal reflection. The guided house's solution specification mentions reversal of actual asymmetry, but its approximately symmetric drawing does not demonstrate that contrast. These practice parts are required introductory practice, and their difficulty comes from viewing direction rather than arithmetic.
findings.assumptions: Students have ordinary prior experience of shapes and views; the supplied teaching does not establish how an asymmetric end changes when viewed from behind. Calculator use is irrelevant.

repair.proposal: Before p4-q1-a, add one guided contrast showing an asymmetric triangular end. Have students sketch its front and back views, then explicitly compare the reversed left-right positions while keeping up unchanged.

findings.doneWhen: Guided teaching visibly distinguishes an unchanged copy from the horizontally reflected back view of an asymmetric end.

findings.finding: Isolate the different effects of doubling cylinder height and doubling radius.
findings.breakdown: The existing practice varies dimensions and representations without a controlled comparison of linear and squared dependence.
findings.checked: Using p24's formula gives 12π, 24π, 96π and 192π cm³, with successive factors 2, 4 and 2. The follow-up diameter gives radius 5 cm and volume 175π cm³. All dimensions are positive and both radius and diameter substitution have been taught.
findings.assumptions: Use exact answers in terms of π; no calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: After p25-q3, add: “Before calculating, predict how each volume compares with the preceding one. Find exact volumes: (a) r = 2 cm, h = 3 cm; (b) r = 2 cm, h = 6 cm; (c) r = 4 cm, h = 6 cm; (d) r = 4 cm, h = 12 cm. What happens when height doubles? When radius doubles?” Expected volumes: 12π, 24π, 96π, 192π cm³. Each transition changes one dimension and holds the other constant. Height doubling doubles volume; radius doubling quadruples it. Follow with: “Find the volume when diameter = 10 cm and height = 7 cm.” Expected answer: 175π cm³.

findings.doneWhen: Students predict and explain the two scaling effects, then solve an unpatterned diameter question.

findings.finding: Explain why an inscribed cylinder occupies the same percentage of every cube.
findings.breakdown: The task generalises the existing numerical comparison through the two taught volume formulas.
findings.checked: For cube side s > 0, the cylinder has radius s/2 and height s. Its volume is πs³/4, while the cube's volume is s³. Their ratio is π/4, giving 25π%, approximately 78.5%. The formulas and the inscribed configuration are already available.
findings.assumptions: The cylinder fits upright with diameter and height equal to the cube side. Elementary algebra is prior knowledge; a calculator is needed only for the decimal percentage.

repair.proposal: After p28-q12, offer: “A cylinder fits exactly inside a cube, with its circular ends touching all four sides of the corresponding square faces. Would a larger cube change the percentage occupied by the cylinder? Justify your answer for a cube of side s > 0.” Expected answer: r = s/2 and h = s, so cylinder volume = πs³/4 and cube volume = s³. The percentage is always 25π%, approximately 78.5%.

findings.doneWhen: Students explain the independence from cube size, including the condition s > 0.

findings.finding: Explain why two conversion routes from cubic metres to millilitres agree.
findings.breakdown: The task distinguishes cubing a length conversion factor from applying a capacity conversion factor.
findings.checked: p30 supplies the cubic conversion factor, p32 supplies capacity factors and p33 supplies volume-capacity equivalences. Both routes give 1,000,000 mL. Capacity factors already compare complete volumes and must not be cubed.
findings.assumptions: The task concerns equivalent measures of volume, with no container geometry or calculator required.

repair.proposal: After p34-q3, offer: “Convert 1 m³ to mL in two ways: first through cm³, then through kL and L. Explain why cubing 100 is appropriate in the first route, while cubing each capacity factor is inappropriate in the second.” Expected answer: 1 m³ = 100³ cm³ = 1,000,000 cm³ = 1,000,000 mL; also 1 m³ = 1 kL = 1000 L = 1,000,000 mL. The factor 100 converts each of three lengths; the capacity factors compare complete volumes.

findings.doneWhen: Students justify both equal results and explain which conversion factors require cubing.

findings.finding: The topic has no opening review of rectangular-prism and cylinder volume calculation, although both are substantial first steps in its worked examples.
findings.breakdown: Students must retrieve and use the appropriate volume formula before applying the recently practised capacity conversions. Conversion practice alone does not rehearse that first step.
findings.checked: p19 and p24 teach the volume formulas, and p29-solids rehearses them two topics earlier. The immediately preceding capacity topic's teaching, guided practice and p34-q3 exercise rehearse conversions, not volume calculation. No review precedes p35-method. The proposed review answers are correct and the four short items fit within one page.
findings.assumptions: The teacher checks the review and responds to recall gaps. Exact cylinder answers avoid dependence on calculator availability.

repair.proposal: Before p35-method, add: “Calculate the volume. Write the formula before substituting. (a) A rectangular prism measuring 5 cm by 3 cm by 8 cm. (b) A rectangular prism with base area 18 m² and height 4 m. (c) A cylinder with radius 3 cm and height 5 cm. (d) A cylinder with radius 2 m and height 7 m. Give cylinder answers in terms of π.” Expected answers: 120 cm³, 72 m³, 45π cm³ and 28π m³.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse both volume calculations before combining them with capacity conversion.

protectedGroups.observation: With the same number of cubes in each layer, volume scales with the number of layers.
protectedGroups.varies: The number of unit-thick layers changes from 1 to 2 to 5.
protectedGroups.invariant: The rectangular base remains 2 by 3, containing six unit cubes per layer.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing the chosen rectangular base changes its area and the corresponding perpendicular height, while the volume remains 180 cm³.
protectedGroups.varies: The highlighted base face and the allocation of the three dimensions between base area and prism height.
protectedGroups.invariant: The same 10 cm by 6 cm by 3 cm rectangular prism and its volume.

protectedGroups.observation: Increasing every edge by 10% increases volume by 33.1%, exposing the difference between linear and volume percentage change.
protectedGroups.varies: The common edge length, from 5 cm to 5.5 cm.
protectedGroups.invariant: Cube shape and the method of multiplying its three dimensions.

protectedGroups.observation: Different adjacent metric unit pairs require different cubic conversion factors even when the starting numerical value is identical.
protectedGroups.varies: The source and destination unit pair; b and c repeat the same conversion.
protectedGroups.invariant: Starting numerical value 2 and conversion from larger to smaller cubic units.

protectedGroups.observation: Reducing the original volume by a factor of ten reduces the converted numerical value by the same factor.
Expressing the same volume in mm³ instead of cm³ introduces an additional factor of 1000.
protectedGroups.varies: Destination unit and number of conversion links.

protectedGroups.observation: A tenfold decrease in the original quantity produces a tenfold decrease after conversion.
Division by 1000 applies whether the result is a whole number, a mixed decimal or less than one litre.
protectedGroups.varies: The input volume and whether it contains a whole number of litre-sized groups.
protectedGroups.invariant: The source unit cm³, target unit L and conversion factor.

protectedGroups.observation: A prism can have different section shapes; the section matches the base when the cutting plane is parallel to it.
protectedGroups.varies: The cutting plane's direction relative to the prism.

protectedGroups.observation: Different cutting directions can both produce rectangles, so section shape must be inferred from the intersection rather than from the trace's appearance alone.
protectedGroups.varies: The cutting plane changes from horizontal to vertical.
protectedGroups.invariant: The rectangular prism and its viewing orientation.

protectedGroups.observation: A fractional quotient must be interpreted differently when purchasing enough bottles and when counting completely filled glasses.
protectedGroups.varies: Whether the whole-number count must provide enough supply or represent only completely filled containers.
protectedGroups.invariant: Divide the total required or available capacity by the capacity of one container.

protectedGroups.observation: Water depth is found by dividing water volume by the horizontal cross-sectional area, regardless of the container's cross-sectional shape.
protectedGroups.varies: The cross-sectional shape and its area calculation; numerical dimensions and water volumes also change.
protectedGroups.invariant: Convert the water volume to compatible cubic units and use depth = volume ÷ base area.

protectedGroups.observation: An asymmetric end makes the left-to-right reversal of the back view observable and moves the top ridge away from the centre.
protectedGroups.varies: The horizontal position of the triangular apex.
protectedGroups.invariant: Prism orientation, triangular end structure and the four requested viewing directions.

protectedGroups.observation: The viewing direction determines which view shows the triangular end.
protectedGroups.invariant: The triangular-prism structure and the four requested views.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing the curved end profile changes the end views while the side and top outlines remain rectangular.
protectedGroups.varies: A full circular end becomes an asymmetric quarter-disc end.
protectedGroups.invariant: A uniform extrusion along the same pictorial depth direction and the four requested views.

protectedGroups.observation: Students increasingly take responsibility for extending a supplied end profile into a prism.
protectedGroups.varies: The end profile and the amount of supplied construction support.
protectedGroups.invariant: Constructing a prism from a supplied polygonal end on a grid.
